title: Why Choose a Similar Game? Give Players a Reason

scenes.title: Why Choose a Similar New Game?
lines: There's already a game people love. If you build something similar, why should people choose it?
We will look at a game that adds mining to movement, and a game about building worlds and racing together, to see how new choices emerge.
We will start with movement under pressure, and see how mining and opening routes add something to that familiar action.

scenes.title: Familiar Rules as a Starting Point
lines: In Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, your weapons attack automatically while you move your character away from enemies.
Moving and avoiding danger while finding the next opportunity give us a starting point for understanding the game.
Creators can start with rules they enjoy, too. By implementing and refining earlier ideas, games have gained new situations and forms of expression.

scenes.title: The Achievement of Finishing a Game
lines: Imagine a small game. You move a character past an obstacle and reach a destination.
Even this simple flow needs work to become a game. It must respond to input, restart after failure, and lead all the way to its ending.

Finishing a game that someone can play from beginning to end, and sharing it with another person, is an achievement. That achievement leads to the next question. Why will a player choose this particular game?

scenes.title: Give Players a Reason to Choose
lines: A game you admire has already shown its appeal. Players know its controls and atmosphere, and know what they can expect from it.
The new game needs actions players want to repeat, and an experience they want to return to.
Some players want more of a familiar experience. When your game adds its own appeal to that expectation, the reason to start again becomes concrete.

scenes.title: Mining Adds a New Purpose to Movement
lines: Let’s return to Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor. As the character reaches a mineral deposit, mining opens up the surrounding space.
Here, enemies to avoid and minerals to collect occupy the same space. Your movement affects both goals at once.
Let’s change the movement goal in our diagram. While choosing a route toward the minerals, you also read the pursuing enemies and possible exits.

When the escape prompt appears, you must reach the escape point within the time limit. Familiar movement and automatic attacks now involve judging mineral targets and terrain. A new purpose changes the choices made through the same movement.

scenes.title: From Player to World Creator
lines: We have seen purpose change movement decisions. The player’s role can also expand. In Super Mario Maker 2, running and jumping provide a familiar starting point.
Now look at the world-building screen. You place land and paths from the start toward the castle, building the structure that connects courses.
Adding branches and placing courses lets you shape what players encounter first and which routes they can choose.
Alongside the enjoyment of mastering jumps, there is enjoyment in creating a route for others. You begin thinking about another person’s play experience.

scenes.title: Racing Alongside Other Players
lines: From designing routes for other players, we can move to the experience of racing through a course together. In multiplayer versus mode, several characters move in response to the same starting signal.
In this mode, the first player to reach the goal wins. While reading the terrain you need to cross, you can also see how far the other players have progressed.
Familiar running and jumping now take place in a race against other people. Who you play with, and under what rules, can become part of the reason to choose a game.

scenes.title: Put Care into Your Own Appeals
lines: Defining a game’s fundamental systems is a demanding part of game design. If you start with established rules, you should put care into refining the other appeals you add. Work carefully on the decisions your new situations will create.
You can refine decisions about mining and escape routes, the creativity of making a world for others, and competition along a shared course. Each can be developed with care.
The goals, controls and on-screen communication need to support the same intended experience. Refine them until players feel that appeal through their actions.

scenes.title: Bring Different Appeals into One Experience
lines: Compare appeal along several dimensions. Look at the recurring action, its purpose, and the player’s role and relationships.
The tension between mining and avoiding enemies, the creativity of building a world, and the competition of racing alongside other players offer different kinds of appeal.
Refining your game’s experience along these dimensions connects familiar rules in a new combination. That combination gives the game its own identity.

scenes.title: Make the Experience Worth Choosing
lines: Inspiration from a game you love can lead to the experience of finishing your own game. Then make the reason to choose it concrete.
What will players do repeatedly? What decisions and feelings will they encounter? Bring the appeals that answer those questions into one coherent experience.
Familiarity provides the starting point. A carefully shaped experience gives players a reason to choose your game.
